scenes.tts: This sea urchin embryo cell is in anaphase: its two sets of chromosomes are moving apart. Now it must cut itself in two, right between them. How does its surface know where the middle is?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, built here and kept for the whole film (16:9, dark background). One large round sea urchin embryo cell seen side-on in section, filling about 75% of frame height, centred a little left of middle. COLOURS BY CONCEPT, fixed for the film and reused in the lesson: microtubules of the spindle and asters BLUE; membrane and cortex a thick GREY rim; RhoA off = small GREY dots spaced along the inner face of the rim; RhoA on = AMBER (so the band is an amber stripe); the actin and myosin ring MAGENTA; the needle a plain WHITE line; chromosomes WHITE. Open on the cell already in anaphase: two white chromosome clusters drifting slowly apart, a blue spindle between them, a blue star-shaped aster at each end, its rays gently flickering. The grey rim breathes slightly. On 'right between', a dashed white line sweeps down through the equator and fades. On 'How does its surface', a white question card fades in at the top: 'How does the surface know where to cut?' Label at top left, size 30, white: 'sea urchin embryo cell'.
scenes.narration: This sea urchin embryo cell is in anaphase: its two sets of chromosomes are moving apart. Now it must cut itself in two, right between them. How does its surface know where the middle is?

scenes.visual: Title 'The Band Before the Furrow' fades in across the lower third for 2 s while the chromosomes keep drifting apart and the aster rays keep flickering; the question card stays at the top.

scenes.tts: The cut happens at the cell surface. There the surface pinches in, making a groove called the furrow. But the thing that marks the middle sits deep inside. It is the spindle, a bundle of microtubules with a star-shaped aster at each end.
scenes.visual: Zoom gently onto the right-hand rim: the grey rim brightens, label 'cell surface' (grey, size 30) beside it, while the grey RhoA-off dots along it drift slightly. On 'pinches in', a faint ghost dent (30% opacity) appears at the equator, label 'furrow' (grey, size 30), then relaxes back to round. Pull back out. On 'deep inside', the blue spindle pulses once and a soft blue glow fills the gap between rim and spindle to show the distance. On 'spindle', label 'spindle' (blue) on the central bundle; on 'aster', label 'aster' (blue) on one star. Chromosomes keep moving apart throughout.
scenes.narration: The cut happens at the cell surface. There the surface pinches in, making a groove called the furrow. But the thing that marks the middle sits deep inside. It is the spindle, a bundle of microtubules with a star-shaped aster at each end.

scenes.tts: There are three simple answers. One: the spindle pulls the surface in directly, by force. Two: an actin ring gathers at the middle on its own. Three: the spindle only sends a signal. The signal marks the surface, and the ring is built under that mark.
scenes.visual: The cell shrinks to the left half of the frame. Three small ghost copies of the cell (40% opacity) slide out in a column on the right, each with a number badge and a 3-word label, each animating its idea in a loop as it is named: 1 'Spindle pulls surface' (blue spindle ends tug the rim inward with blue arrows, no amber anywhere); 2 'Ring comes first' (a magenta ring forms at the equator with nothing else changing); 3 'Signal, then ring' (no arrows; an amber stripe appears on the rim first, then a magenta ring under it). All three keep looping quietly.
scenes.narration: There are three simple answers. One: the spindle pulls the surface in directly, by force. Two: an actin ring gathers at the middle on its own. Three: the spindle only sends a signal. The signal marks the surface, and the ring is built under that mark.

scenes.tts: To tell them apart, researchers watched a switch protein called RhoA. RhoA is on when it holds G T P, and off when it holds G D P. They added a glowing probe that sticks only to switched-on RhoA.
scenes.caption: To tell them apart, researchers watched a switch protein called RhoA. RhoA is on when it holds GTP, and off when it holds GDP. They added a glowing probe that sticks only to switched-on RhoA.
scenes.visual: Inset box at top right (the ghost column dims to 25%): a grey rounded block 'RhoA' holding a small grey tag 'GDP' (off). The tag pops out and a tag 'GTP' snaps in; the block turns AMBER (on). It flips back and forth twice in rhythm with the words. On 'glowing probe', a small green-white crescent labelled 'probe' drifts in, ignores the grey block, and docks only on the amber block, which then glows. Labelled blocks only, no molecular structure.
scenes.narration: To tell them apart, researchers watched a switch protein called RhoA. RhoA is on when it holds GTP, and off when it holds GDP. They added a glowing probe that sticks only to switched-on RhoA.

scenes.visual: Show, then tell. The inset fades. Back on the full cell: along the inner face of the rim at the equator, top and bottom, the grey dots begin turning amber one after another until a bright amber stripe sits across the equator on both sides. The rim is still perfectly round: no dent yet. A white clock icon in the corner starts ticking.

scenes.tts: A band of active RhoA, shown here in amber, lights up just under the membrane. One to four minutes later, the furrow starts underneath it. The same order was seen in frog embryos. The mark comes before the cut.
scenes.visual: The amber stripe holds and shimmers; on 'shown here in amber', a small key appears in the corner, an amber dot labelled 'active RhoA' (size 28), and stays for the rest of the film. On 'One to four minutes later', the clock icon spins and a small timeline bar along the bottom fills: first an amber tick 'band', then a gap labelled '1-4 min', then a grey tick 'furrow'. Only then does the rim start to dent inward under the stripe (a shallow notch on each side). On 'frog embryos', a small second cell (label 'frog embryo') appears at bottom right playing the same order: amber stripe, then dent. Ghost 1 ('Spindle pulls surface') dims to half opacity, not yet removed.
scenes.narration: A band of active RhoA, shown here in amber, lights up just under the membrane. One to four minutes later, the furrow starts underneath it. The same order was seen in frog embryos. The mark comes before the cut.

scenes.tts: Next, they blocked actin assembly with a drug, so no ring could be built. In sea urchin embryos, the amber band still formed. So the signal does not need the ring. Answer two is out.
scenes.visual: Rewind the cell to round with no stripe (a quick reverse wipe). A red label 'actin blocked' with a red bar-headed line appears beside the cell; any magenta filaments that start to form at the equator flash red and vanish. Then the grey dots at the equator turn amber again, and the amber stripe forms just as before, with no magenta and no dent. On 'Answer two is out', ghost 2 ('Ring comes first') gets a red cross and slides off-frame.
scenes.narration: Next, they blocked actin assembly with a drug, so no ring could be built. In sea urchin embryos, the amber band still formed. So the signal does not need the ring. Answer two is out.

scenes.tts: Now the decisive test. This cell has already begun to furrow. A blunt needle pushes the spindle to one side. What moves first: the furrow, the amber band, or nothing?
scenes.visual: The cell is furrowing: amber stripe at the equator, shallow notches in the rim under it. A plain white needle enters from the upper left and presses on the cell, and the blue spindle with both asters slides slowly to the right, so its middle is now well right of the old stripe. The needle withdraws. On 'What moves first', a white question card fades in at the top: 'What moves first?' with three small options below it: 'furrow', 'amber band', 'nothing'.
scenes.narration: Now the decisive test. This cell has already begun to furrow. A blunt needle pushes the spindle to one side. What moves first: the furrow, the amber band, or nothing?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. The question card and its three options stay on screen. The cell holds with the spindle displaced right, the old amber stripe and notches still at the old equator; aster rays flicker gently and a faint pulse travels along the rim so the frame is not frozen.

scenes.tts: Over a few minutes, active RhoA gathers over the spindle's new middle. Only then does the furrow follow it there. The band leads, and the furrow follows. That order argues against the spindle simply dragging the surface, and it supports answer three: signal first.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. The clock icon ticks. The old amber stripe slowly fades to grey dots while, over the spindle's new middle, grey dots turn amber one by one into a new stripe. Only after the new stripe is complete do the old notches relax and new notches dent the rim under the new stripe. Corner label 'schematic'. On 'argues against', ghost 1 ('Spindle pulls surface') fades to 15% and slides off without a cross; on 'answer three', ghost 3 ('Signal, then ring') glows amber and stays.
scenes.narration: Over a few minutes, active RhoA gathers over the spindle's new middle. Only then does the furrow follow it there. The band leads, and the furrow follows. That order argues against the spindle simply dragging the surface, and it supports answer three: signal first.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule for these embryo cells. The cut goes where the anaphase microtubules place a band of active RhoA. Move the microtubules, and the band moves first. The furrow follows.
scenes.visual: Ghost 3 slides back into the cell and merges with it. Along a lower strip, three labelled blocks build left to right with arrows between them, each lighting as it is named: blue 'microtubules', then amber 'RhoA band', then grey 'furrow'. Above the cell the rule fades in, size 34, white with 'microtubules' in blue and 'RhoA' in amber: 'In these embryo cells, microtubules place the RhoA band; the furrow follows.' The cell itself repeats the needle shift in miniature, slowly: spindle moves, stripe rebuilds, notch follows.
scenes.narration: Here is the rule for these embryo cells. The cut goes where the anaphase microtubules place a band of active RhoA. Move the microtubules, and the band moves first. The furrow follows.

scenes.tts: Under the band, active RhoA turns on formins and promotes myosin two. Formins build long actin filaments. Myosin two, a motor, pulls those filaments past each other. In its simplest picture, the result is a ring that tightens like a drawstring.
scenes.caption: Under the band, active RhoA turns on formins and promotes myosin II. Formins build long actin filaments. Myosin II, a motor, pulls those filaments past each other. In its simplest picture, the result is a ring that tightens like a drawstring.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the amber stripe at the top of the equator (about 2x). Small block 'formin' (magenta outline) sits on the membrane and extrudes a long magenta bead-chain filament as it is named. A second filament runs the other way. A small two-headed block 'myosin II' (magenta) grabs both and walks, sliding them past each other so their ends draw together. Pull back: a magenta ring now girdles the cell under the amber stripe and starts to tighten; the furrow deepens. One word label appears once, 'drawstring', then fades.
scenes.narration: Under the band, active RhoA turns on formins and promotes myosin II. Formins build long actin filaments. Myosin II, a motor, pulls those filaments past each other. In its simplest picture, the result is a ring that tightens like a drawstring.

scenes.visual: Show, then tell. Pull back to the whole cell: the magenta ring keeps tightening and the furrow deepens from both sides until the cell is two rounded daughters joined by a thin neck. No narration; the motion is the point.

scenes.tts: Now the two daughters are joined only by a thin bridge. Cutting that bridge is a separate job. One question stays open: how do microtubules deep inside switch on a protein at the membrane? But where the cut went was settled earlier, where the microtubules placed the band.
scenes.visual: Hold on the two rounded daughters, each with its chromosome cluster, joined by a thin grey bridge with a short blue bundle inside it; the daughters breathe gently. A small grey label 'bridge' points to it and pulses on 'separate job'. On 'One question stays open', a white question card fades in at the top: 'Microtubules inside, RhoA at the membrane: how?' and a faint dotted blue line runs from the bridge's blue bundle toward the rim, with a white '?' on it. On 'settled earlier', the question card dims, a brief amber after-glow flashes once at the bridge's position and the three-block strip 'microtubules, RhoA band, furrow' re-lights in order underneath.
scenes.narration: Now the two daughters are joined only by a thin bridge. Cutting that bridge is a separate job. One question stays open: how do microtubules deep inside switch on a protein at the membrane? But where the cut went was settled earlier, where the microtubules placed the band.

scenes.line: In these embryo cells, microtubules place the RhoA band; the furrow follows.
scenes.visual: End card over the two daughters (dimmed to 30%): the take-home line, size 40, white with 'microtubules' in blue and 'RhoA' in amber: 'In these embryo cells, microtubules place the RhoA band; the furrow follows.' The bridge still pulses gently.
